chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Abd al-Malik ibn Utbah from Isḥaq ibn ʿAmmār from Yaḥyā ibn Abi al-ʿAlāʾ from Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him) who said:

The one who fasts in the month of Ramadan while traveling is like the one who breaks the fast while residing [at home]. Then he said: 'Indeed, a man came to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) and said: O Messenger of Allah, should I fast the month of Ramadan while traveling? He said: No. He said: O Messenger of Allah, it is easy for me [to do so]. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: Indeed, Allah granted a concession (voluntarily gave up a right) to the sick and travelers of His ummah by allowing them to break the fast in the month of Ramadan. Would any of you like that if he gave a charity, it would be returned to him?'

key_terms.تَصَدَّقَ: Granted a concession/Voluntarily gave up a right

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling and wisdom behind a traveler fasting in Ramadan according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes that fasting while traveling during Ramadan is not merely permissible but often preferred, equating the traveler who fasts to one who breaks it at home to highlight the loss of the specific divine concession (rukhsah). He illustrates this by recounting the Prophet’s response to a companion who insisted on fasting despite it being easy for him, comparing Allah’s gift of exemption to a charity; if one rejects the easier option (breaking fast) when the concession is intended for relief, it is akin to having that charity returned, thereby forfeiting the spiritual benefit of the ease granted. This narration underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle that divine concessions are meant to be utilized for mercy, not necessarily rejected in favor of stricter asceticism unless there is a specific reason.
